newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Outraged Serbian opposition calls for protests.
newsitem.headline: Outraged Serbian opposition calls for protests.

text.p: Serbian opposition parties urged supporters on Wednesday to protest in the streets to defend their victory in local elections, accusing the authorities of trying to annul the results through fraud.
The opposition coalition organised demonstrations in the capital Belgrade and several major towns to demand that the ruling Socialists accept their unprecedented defeat.
Electoral officials on Tuesday confirmed the opposition's victory in Belgrade, a stunning blow to the Socialists led by President Slobodan Milosevic.
But authorities had failed to announce official results in other towns where the opposition said it also scored clear majorities. The Socialists, as expected, won federal elections two weeks ago.
As tension mounted, the three leaders of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition and other opposition members of parliament went on hunger strike in Belgrade.
Some 2,000 demonstrators gathered outside the building and chanted against Milosevic's nine-year rule.
The 66 opposition representatives said they would stay inside the Serbian parliament in Belgrade "until the democratically expressed desires of the people are fulfilled," said a coalition statement.
From the fifth floor window, Vuk Draskovic, one of the Zajedno leaders, addressed the crowd.

"I appeal to all of you to defend our electoral will, to go out into the streets and by your numbers, your strength and the perseverance you will show over the coming days, force the people who organised this completely unprecedented election fraud to see reason," said Draskovic, his voice hoarse.

He read a letter to Milosevic calling on the former communist party leader to abide by the country's constitution. Draskovic led street demonstrations for press freedom in 1991 which Milosevic crushed with police and the army.
The opposition coalition had appealed to United States and the European Union to support their protests and condemn attempts to reverse the election results, Draskovic told reporters.
Western diplomats view Milosevic as a guarantor of stability in the region after he signed the peace treaty that ended the Bosnian war last year.
Draskovic said the West's silence was "shameful" and said a democratically-elected opposition would be more capable of bringing real peace to the Balkans.
"New people who were from the beginning...against ethnic cleansing and war crimes can establish a stable peace, reconciliation and repentance in the Balkans," he said.
Socialist authorities brought in police with riot gear to protect town halls in several towns but there were no violent clashes reported late on Wednesday.

"In practically all towns in Serbia where we have won, results are being cancelled, exactly to the extent it is necessary to cancel our victory and to give it to those who have lost the elections," Zoran Djindjic, head of the opposition Democratic Party, told reporters earlier.
Electoral commissions by law were required to confirm official results by Tuesday evening, 48 hours after polling stations closed.
But the commissions have cited unspecified irregularities in various municipalities where the opposition won a majority and said another round of voting was required.
